topics.name: Parkinson’s disease
topics.kicker: Brain disease that affects movement · Linked to loss of dopamine-making cells
topics.briefing: Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that slowly makes movement harder, often starting with a shaking hand, stiff muscles, or slow steps. It happens as nerve cells in a small, dark region of the brain, the substantia nigra, are slowly lost, leaving too little dopamine, a chemical messenger that helps control movement. English surgeon James Parkinson described it in 1817, and a medicine called levodopa, which the brain turns into dopamine, helps many people with the disease.
topics.answerHtml: Parkinson’s disease (accept Parkinson disease or paralysis agitans; prompt on parkinsonism or shaking palsy; do not accept “Alzheimer’s disease” or “Huntington’s disease”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1912, Friedrich Lewy described round clumps of protein inside the nerve cells of people with this disease, and those clumps are now called Lewy bodies. They are made largely of a protein called alpha-synuclein [“sih-NOO-klee-in”].
tossups.r: In this disease, dopamine-making cells in the brain are lost. For 10 points, name this movement disorder that often causes a tremor in a resting hand.

tossups.p: Arvid Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in medicine partly for showing that animals given the drug reserpine became slow and stiff, much like people with this disease, until they received L-DOPA. His work showed that dopamine is a brain messenger in its own right.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease in which dopamine-making brain cells are slowly lost, causing tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: In the book _Awakenings_, Oliver Sacks described how the drug L-DOPA in 1969 briefly brought back movement to patients who had barely been able to move for decades because of a condition with this disease’s symptoms. Robin Williams starred in a 1990 film of that story.
tossups.r: Doctors give L-DOPA for this disease because the brain turns it into dopamine. For 10 points, name this movement disorder.

tossups.p: In 1960, Oleh Hornykiewicz [“hor-nee-KEH-vitch”] found that the brains of people who had this disease contained far less dopamine than normal. Later that decade, George Cotzias [“KOT-see-us”] showed that large doses of levodopa taken by mouth could ease this disease’s symptoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes tremors, stiff muscles, and slow movement.

tossups.p: People with this disease may develop micrographia [“my-kroh-GRAF-ee-uh”], handwriting that becomes smaller and more cramped, and their faces may show less expression. Losing the sense of smell can be one of this disease’s earliest signs, years before any movement problems.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that causes a shaking tremor and slow movement, named for an English surgeon.

tossups.p: In deep brain stimulation, surgeons place thin wires in a region such as the subthalamic [“sub-thuh-LAM-ik”] nucleus to send gentle electrical pulses that calm this disease’s tremors. Many people with this disease take levodopa together with carbidopa, which stops the body from turning levodopa into dopamine before it reaches the brain.
tossups.r: This disease is linked to the loss of dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: A world awareness day for this disease is held on April 11, the birthday of the English surgeon who described it in _An Essay on the Shaking Palsy_ in 1817. Decades later, the French doctor Jean-Martin Charcot [“shar-KOH”] suggested renaming the disease after that surgeon.
tossups.r: Muhammad Ali was diagnosed with it in 1984. For 10 points, name this disease of tremors and slow movement.

tossups.p: The pigment neuromelanin [“noor-oh-MEL-uh-nin”] darkens the brain region hit hardest by this disease, a region whose Latin name means “black substance.” That region of the midbrain normally sends dopamine to the basal ganglia, which help control movement.
tossups.r: That region is the substantia nigra [“sub-STAN-shuh NYE-gruh”]. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors and stiffness.

tossups.p: The actor who starred in the _Back to the Future_ movies revealed in 1998 that he had this disease, and in 2000 he started a foundation to fund research on it. Boxer Muhammad Ali, who was diagnosed with this disease in 1984, lit the Olympic flame at the 1996 Atlanta Games.
tossups.r: It is linked to the loss of dopamine-making brain cells. For 10 points, name this disease that causes tremors, stiffness, and slow movement.

tossups.p: Doctors call the classic shaking of this disease a “pill-rolling” tremor, because the thumb and fingers rub together as if rolling a small pill between them. That tremor is usually strongest when the hand is resting and fades when the person reaches for something.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease linked to the loss of dopamine-making neurons in the brain.

tossups.p: Medical students remember this disease’s four main signs with the word TRAP: tremor, rigidity, akinesia [“ay-kih-NEE-zhuh”] or slowness, and postural instability, which means trouble with balance. Many people with this disease walk with short, shuffling steps.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this movement disorder linked to a loss of the brain chemical dopamine.

tossups.p: Doctors cannot treat this disease with dopamine itself, because dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Instead they use levodopa, which crosses into the brain and is then converted into dopamine.
tossups.r: This disease damages dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra. For 10 points, name this disease that often begins with a tremor in one hand.

tossups.p: This disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer’s, and it usually begins after age 60. Unlike Huntington’s disease, which is caused by a change in a single inherited gene, this disease usually has no single known cause.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that slowly makes movement harder, often starting with a tremor in one hand.

tossups.p: In this disease, a shortage of dopamine reaching the striatum [“stry-AY-tum”], a part of the basal ganglia, makes it hard for the brain to start and smoothly control movements. Some people with this disease suddenly “freeze” in place when trying to walk through a doorway.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disorder whose symptoms include a resting tremor and stiff muscles.

tossups.p: Pope John Paul II and Janet Reno, the U.S. attorney general from 1993 to 2001, both had this disease. Some people with this disease develop a softer, quieter voice, along with stiff muscles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this brain disease that causes tremors and slow movement and is often treated with levodopa.

Treated with levodopa (L-DOPA), which the brain turns into dopamine
Hits the substantia nigra (“black substance”), a dark region of the midbrain
Its tremor is strongest at rest: a “pill-rolling” motion of the thumb and fingers
First described in _An Essay on the Shaking Palsy_ (1817)

Too little dopamine reaches the basal ganglia, so it is hard to start and smoothly control movements

Many people with it walk with short, shuffling steps and may “freeze” in doorways
Levodopa is often given with carbidopa so more of it reaches the brain

Deep brain stimulation sends gentle electrical pulses to areas like the subthalamic nucleus to calm tremors

Its awareness day, April 11, is the describer’s birthday; Jean-Martin Charcot suggested naming it after him
Arvid Carlsson (Nobel Prize, 2000) showed dopamine is a brain messenger; L-DOPA reversed slowness in animals given reserpine
In 1960, Oleh Hornykiewicz found far less dopamine than normal in the brains of people who had it
In the 1960s, George Cotzias showed that large doses of levodopa by mouth eased its symptoms
Oliver Sacks’s _Awakenings_ tells how L-DOPA briefly restored movement to patients with similar symptoms in 1969; the 1990 film starred Robin Williams
The pigment neuromelanin gives the substantia nigra its dark color

The second most common neurodegenerative disease after Alzheimer’s; it usually begins after age 60

trap.title: Which brain disease?
trap.body: Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, and Huntington’s diseases all slowly damage the brain, so their clues get mixed up. Alzheimer’s mainly affects memory and is marked by plaques and tangles; Huntington’s is caused by a single inherited gene and brings sudden, jerky movements. Don’t be fooled by Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome either: it is a heart rhythm condition with no link to this disease.
trap.fix: Dopamine, the substantia nigra, Lewy bodies, levodopa, a resting “pill-rolling” tremor, or Michael J. Fox mean Parkinson’s disease. Memory loss with plaques and tangles means Alzheimer’s; one inherited gene with jerky movements means Huntington’s.
trap.line: Real answer line: Parkinson’s disease (accept Parkinson disease; prompt on parkinsonism; do not accept “Alzheimer’s disease”)

topics.name: Leprosy
topics.kicker: Bacterial disease of the skin and nerves · Curable with multidrug therapy
topics.briefing: Leprosy, also called Hansen’s disease, is an infection caused by a slow-growing bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis. It mainly affects the skin and the nerves of the hands, feet, and face, and it can take years to show symptoms. For centuries, people with leprosy were feared and forced to live apart, but since the 1980s a combination of antibiotics called multidrug therapy has cured millions of people.
topics.answerHtml: Leprosy (accept Hansen’s disease; prompt on Mycobacterium leprae; do not accept “tuberculosis”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The bacterium that causes this disease still cannot be grown on lab dishes, so scientists grow it in mouse footpads and in nine-banded armadillos, whose cool bodies suit it. In people, that bacterium prefers cooler parts of the body, such as the skin and the nerves just beneath it.
tossups.r: Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified that bacterium in 1873. For 10 points, name this disease that can damage the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: In 1941, Guy Faget began treating patients with this disease using a drug called Promin at a national hospital in Carville, Louisiana, a success called the “Miracle at Carville.” A related, cheaper pill, dapsone, later became a standard treatment for this disease.
tossups.r: It is now cured with a mix of antibiotics called multidrug therapy. For 10 points, name this bacterial disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: A Belgian priest named Damien [“DAY-mee-un”] cared for people with this disease at Kalaupapa [“kah-lah-oo-PAH-pah”] on the Hawaiian island of Molokai and caught it himself; he was declared a saint in 2009. Mother Marianne Cope, who also served people with this disease on Molokai, was declared a saint in 2012.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis.

tossups.p: Surgeon Paul Brand showed that much of the damage linked to this disease comes from injuries that people do not notice, because the disease harms the nerves that sense pain. Despite a common myth, this disease does not make fingers and toes simply fall off.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease, curable with multidrug therapy, that can numb the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Baldwin IV became King of Jerusalem in 1174 at age 13 even though he had this disease, and three years later he defeated Saladin at the Battle of Montgisard [“mohn-zhee-ZAR”]. In medieval Europe, many people with this disease were made to live apart in special houses outside towns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves, which is now curable with antibiotics.

tossups.p: In Lew Wallace’s 1880 novel _Ben-Hur_, the hero’s mother and sister catch this disease while in prison and are later healed. The Gospels describe Jesus healing people with this disease, which was greatly feared in the ancient world.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease that affects the skin and nerves and is now curable with multidrug therapy.

tossups.p: Raoul Follereau [“foh-luh-ROH”] of France started a world awareness day for this disease in 1954, held on the last Sunday of January, near the anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi’s death. Gandhi was known for caring for people with this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bacterial disease, curable with multidrug therapy, that can damage nerves in the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Doctors divide this disease into a milder “tuberculoid” form, with only a few light-colored, numb skin patches, and a more severe form with many patches and huge numbers of bacteria. Its bacterium multiplies very slowly, so symptoms can take years to appear.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a bacterium related to the tuberculosis germ.

tossups.p: Like the tuberculosis germ, the bacterium behind this disease has a waxy cell wall that holds on to red dye in an “acid-fast” stain. That bacterium divides only about once every two weeks, far more slowly than most bacteria.
tossups.r: In 1873, Norwegian doctor Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified it, one of the first germs linked to a human disease. For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: In the southern United States, nine-banded armadillos carry the bacterium that causes this disease and have passed it to some people. Most people who are exposed to that bacterium never get sick, because their immune systems fight it off.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease, now curable with a mix of antibiotics, that affects the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: The World Health Organization’s multidrug therapy for this disease combines dapsone, rifampicin [“rih-FAM-pih-sin”], and clofazimine [“kloh-FAZ-ih-meen”], and it has been given free of charge around the world since 1995. That treatment has cured millions of people.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease caused by a slow-growing bacterium related to the one that causes tuberculosis.

tossups.p: India reports more new cases of this disease each year than any other country, followed by Brazil and Indonesia. In 2000, the World Health Organization announced that this disease had been eliminated “as a public health problem” worldwide, meaning fewer than one case for every 10,000 people.
tossups.r: Its germ is a cousin of the tuberculosis germ. For 10 points, name this disease that can numb the hands and feet.

tossups.p: Many patients and doctors prefer another name for this disease, one that honors the Norwegian doctor who found its cause, because its usual name carries centuries of fear and unfair treatment. In the 1900s, many Americans with this disease were sent to live at a hospital in Carville, Louisiana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease of the skin and nerves, caused by a bacterium related to tuberculosis.

tossups.p: Starting in 1866, the Kingdom of Hawaii sent people with this disease to live in isolation on the Kalaupapa peninsula of Molokai, a place cut off by towering sea cliffs. That settlement became a national historical park in 1980.
tossups.r: A Belgian priest, Father Damien, served the people there. For 10 points, name this bacterial disease of the skin and nerves.

tossups.p: Medieval hospitals for people with this disease were often called lazar houses, after Lazarus, a poor, sick man in one of Jesus’s parables. In the Hebrew Bible, the word tzaraath [“tsah-RAH-aht”], often translated as the name of this disease, covers several different skin conditions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease, caused by a bacterium related to tuberculosis, that can damage nerves.

clues.t: A bacterial disease that mainly affects the skin and nerves
Also named for Norwegian doctor Gerhard Armauer Hansen, who identified its bacterium in 1873
Damages nerves, so people can lose feeling in their hands and feet
Curable with multidrug therapy, a combination of antibiotics
Father Damien cared for people with it on the Hawaiian island of Molokai
Its bacterium is a close relative of the one that causes tuberculosis
Its bacterium multiplies very slowly, so symptoms can take years to appear
Its bacterium prefers cooler parts of the body, like the skin and the nerves just beneath it
Nine-banded armadillos in the southern United States carry it and have passed it to some people
Most people exposed to its bacterium never get sick, because their immune systems fight it off
From 1866, Hawaii sent people with it to live in isolation on the Kalaupapa peninsula of Molokai
Despite a myth, it does not make fingers and toes fall off; unnoticed injuries cause much of the damage
Comes in a milder “tuberculoid” form with a few numb skin patches and a more severe form with many
For centuries, people with it were feared and made to live apart from everyone else
The Gospels describe Jesus healing people with it
Its bacterium can’t be grown on lab dishes, so scientists grow it in mouse footpads and armadillos
In 1941, Guy Faget’s use of the drug Promin at a hospital in Carville, Louisiana, was called the “Miracle at Carville”
Dapsone became a standard pill; WHO’s multidrug therapy adds rifampicin and clofazimine and has been free since 1995
Surgeon Paul Brand showed that much of its damage comes from injuries people can’t feel
Baldwin IV, King of Jerusalem from 1174, had it, yet defeated Saladin at Montgisard in 1177
In Lew Wallace’s _Ben-Hur_ (1880), the hero’s mother and sister catch it in prison and are later healed
Raoul Follereau started its world day in 1954, held on the last Sunday of January, near the anniversary of Gandhi’s death
Its bacterium’s waxy cell wall holds red dye in an “acid-fast” stain
India reports the most new cases each year, followed by Brazil and Indonesia
In 2000, WHO declared it eliminated “as a public health problem” worldwide: under one case per 10,000 people
Damien was declared a saint in 2009, and Mother Marianne Cope, who also served on Molokai, in 2012
Medieval hospitals for people with it were called lazar houses, after Lazarus in one of Jesus’s parables
The Hebrew Bible’s word tzaraath, often translated as its name, covers several different skin conditions

trap.title: Not tuberculosis!
trap.body: The germ that causes this disease is a close cousin of the tuberculosis germ: both are slow-growing, acid-fast bacteria, and their discoveries came only nine years apart (Hansen in 1873, Robert Koch in 1882). Answer lines want the disease, so naming the germ may only earn a prompt. Also remember that in the Bible, the word translated as “leprosy” covered several skin conditions.
trap.fix: Numb skin patches, hands and feet that lose feeling, armadillos, Molokai, Father Damien, Hansen, or Carville mean leprosy. Coughing, the lungs, or Robert Koch mean tuberculosis. If you say the germ’s name, be ready to name the disease.
trap.line: Real answer line: Leprosy (accept Hansen’s disease; prompt on Mycobacterium leprae; do not accept “tuberculosis”)

topics.name: Species
topics.kicker: Basic unit of classification · Members can interbreed and have fertile young
topics.dates: Two-part names became standard with Linnaeus in 1753
topics.briefing: A species is a group of living things so alike that they can mate and have young that can someday have young of their own. Lions are one species and tigers another, and while a horse and a donkey can produce a mule, mules are almost always sterile. Since Carl Linnaeus in the 1700s, every species gets a two-part Latin name, like Homo sapiens for humans: first the genus, then a second word for the species.
topics.answerHtml: Species (accept biological species; prompt on taxon; do not accept “genus” or “speciation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ernst Mayr’s 1942 definition of this term describes groups of populations that actually or potentially interbreed and are reproductively isolated from other such groups. That “biological” concept of this term does not work well for organisms that reproduce without mating, such as bacteria.
tossups.r: Members of one of these groups can mate and produce fertile offspring. For 10 points, name this basic rank of classification, which comes just below genus.

tossups.p: Ensatina [“en-suh-TEE-nuh”] salamanders form a “ring” of populations around California’s Central Valley in which neighbors can interbreed, but the two ends of the ring, which meet in southern California, rarely do. That pattern makes it hard to decide where one of these groups ends and the next begins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this taxonomic rank, just below genus, whose members can mate and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Hybrid sterility is a postzygotic [“post-zye-GOT-ik”] barrier that keeps two of these groups separate even when they mate and produce offspring. Because the mules born to horses and donkeys are almost always sterile, horses and donkeys count as two different examples of this rank.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of biological classification, whose members can breed and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Prezygotic [“pree-zye-GOT-ik”] barriers, such as different mating seasons or different courtship displays, can stop two of these groups from interbreeding before an egg is ever fertilized. Eastern and Western meadowlarks look almost alike but are separate examples of this rank, partly because they sing different songs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rank of classification, below genus, given by the two words of a scientific name like Homo sapiens.

tossups.p: A single preserved specimen called a holotype [“HOL-oh-type”] serves as the official reference for the scientific name of one of these groups. A scientist who discovers a new one of these groups must publish a formal description of it along with a Latin-style name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed, named with a genus plus a second word.

tossups.p: In a 1753 book on plants, Carl Linnaeus made it standard to name each of these groups with two Latin words: a capitalized genus followed by a lowercase “specific epithet.” That naming system, whose names are printed in italics, is called binomial nomenclature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most specific basic rank of classification, such as Homo sapiens for humans.

tossups.p: A 2011 study estimated that Earth holds about 8.7 million of these groups of organisms whose cells have a nucleus, most of which have never been described. Beetles have more named examples of this rank than any other order of animals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can mate and have fertile offspring.

tossups.p: Harris’s antelope squirrel lives south of the Grand Canyon, while the closely related white-tailed antelope squirrel lives north of it, a classic case of a barrier splitting a population into two of these groups. That kind of split, caused by geographic separation, is called “allopatric” [“al-oh-PAT-rik”].
tossups.r: New ones form through a process called speciation. For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification just below genus.

tossups.p: A 1973 law signed by Richard Nixon protects threatened and endangered examples of this rank in the United States, and the bald eagle was taken off that law’s list in 2007 after its numbers recovered. The California condor is among the groups protected by that law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

tossups.p: Ecologist Robert Paine removed Pisaster [“pih-ZAS-ter”] sea stars from tide pools and found that mussels took over, showing that some of these groups have an outsized effect on their ecosystems. Paine called such a group a “keystone,” after the center stone that holds up an arch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, named by the two words of a scientific name like Tyrannosaurus rex.

tossups.p: Under the phylogenetic [“fye-loh-juh-NET-ik”] concept of this term, one of these groups is the smallest set of organisms that share a common ancestor and can be told apart from all others. Because biologists use many competing definitions of this term, their debate is called this term’s “problem.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic rank of classification, whose members can usually mate and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, and with her, that group at this level of classification was gone forever. The dodo of the island of Mauritius is another example of this rank that has gone extinct.
tossups.r: In the memory aid “King Philip Came Over For Good Soup,” this rank is the “Soup.” For 10 points, name this most specific basic rank in taxonomy.

tossups.p: In an 1855 paper written in Sarawak on the island of Borneo, Alfred Russel Wallace argued that each new one of these groups appears near a closely related one that already exists.
tossups.r: Four years later, Charles Darwin published a book explaining how these groups originate. For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification whose members can interbreed.

tossups.p: The tenth edition of Carl Linnaeus’s _Systema Naturae_, published in 1758, is the official starting point for scientific names of animals at this rank, including Homo sapiens, which means “wise man.”
tossups.r: This rank sits just below genus. For 10 points, name this rank whose members can interbreed and have fertile young.

tossups.p: Lions and tigers can produce hybrid cubs called ligers in zoos, but the two cats do not interbreed in the wild, so they remain separate examples of this rank. Polar bears and grizzly bears, though, have occasionally had hybrid cubs in the wild.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this basic unit of classification, whose members can interbreed and have fertile young.

clues.t: A group whose members can mate and produce fertile offspring
The most specific basic rank in taxonomy, just below genus
Its scientific name has two parts, a genus and a second word, as in Homo sapiens for humans

Carl Linnaeus made two-word Latin names standard in a 1753 book on plants
New ones form through a process called speciation
Kept apart by reproductive isolation: prezygotic barriers before fertilization and postzygotic barriers after
Abbreviated “sp.” for one and “spp.” for several
The dodo of Mauritius is one extinct example
Lions and tigers can produce ligers in zoos but stay separate because they don’t interbreed in the wild
Eastern and Western meadowlarks look alike but are separate, partly because they sing different songs
A 1973 U.S. law signed by Richard Nixon protects endangered ones
Ernst Mayr’s 1942 “biological” concept: populations that interbreed and are isolated from others; it fails for bacteria and others that don’t mate
Ensatina salamanders form a “ring” around California’s Central Valley whose two ends rarely interbreed
A single preserved holotype specimen is the official reference for a scientific name
The second word of the two-part name is called the specific epithet
A 2011 study estimated about 8.7 million kinds of organisms with nucleus-containing cells, most still undescribed
Beetles have more named examples than any other order of animals
Two antelope squirrels, split by the Grand Canyon, show “allopatric” (geographic) separation
The bald eagle was taken off the endangered list in 2007; the California condor is protected under the same 1973 law
Robert Paine’s sea star experiments showed that some are “keystone” groups with outsized effects
The phylogenetic concept defines it by shared ancestry; arguments over definitions are called this term’s “problem”
Martha, the last known passenger pigeon, died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914
Alfred Russel Wallace’s 1855 paper from Sarawak said each new one appears near a closely related one
The 10th edition of Linnaeus’s _Systema Naturae_ (1758) is the starting point for animal names; Homo sapiens means “wise man”

trap.title: Species, genus, or speciation?
trap.body: In a two-part name like Homo sapiens, the first word is the genus, the rank just above, and the species is named by both words together. Speciation, the process that forms new species, is a separate answer line, and so is genus. Breeds don’t count either: every dog breed belongs to the same species.
trap.fix: “Members can interbreed,” “fertile offspring,” or “the rank just below genus” means species. “The rank above,” or the capitalized first word of a scientific name, means genus. If the question asks for “this process” that splits one group into two, say speciation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Species (do not accept “genus” or “speciation”)

topics.name: Gallbladder
topics.kicker: Small pouch under the liver · Stores bile and squeezes it out to digest fat
topics.dates: Holds only a few tablespoons of bile
topics.briefing: The gallbladder, a small, pear-shaped pouch tucked under the liver, stores and concentrates bile, a greenish fluid the liver makes all day long. When a fatty meal arrives, a hormone called CCK makes it squeeze bile into the small intestine, where bile breaks fat into tiny droplets. Sometimes bile hardens into gallstones, and doctors can remove the whole organ, because people can live without it.
topics.answerHtml: Gallbladder (accept gall bladder; prompt on biliary system; do not accept “liver,” “pancreas,” or “bile duct”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1882, the German surgeon Carl Langenbuch [“LAHNG-en-bookh”] performed the first successful operation to remove this organ, which is now one of the most common surgeries. People can live without this organ, because the liver can still send its fluid straight to the intestine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ that stores bile made by the liver.

tossups.p: The hormone cholecystokinin [“koh-luh-sis-toh-KY-nin”], whose name means “bile sac mover,” is released by the duodenum when fatty food arrives and makes this organ contract. At the same time, the sphincter of Oddi [“ODD-ee”] relaxes so this organ’s contents can flow into the intestine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and releases it to help digest fats.

tossups.p: Horses, deer, and rats all lack this organ, so bile flows straight from their livers into their intestines. In humans, this organ makes the bile it holds more concentrated by absorbing water from it between meals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ tucked under the liver, where gallstones can form.

tossups.p: A medicine that can slowly dissolve some of the stones that form in this organ is named for bears, because its main chemical was first found in bear bile. Most of those stones are made largely of cholesterol, while others are dark “pigment” stones.
tossups.r: Those stones are called gallstones. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile from the liver.

tossups.p: King Goujian [“GOH-jyen”] of Yue is said to have tasted the bitter fluid stored in this organ every day to remind himself of a defeat, a story behind a Chinese saying about perseverance. In Chinese, having a “big” one of these organs means being bold or brave.
tossups.r: The liver makes that fluid, called bile. For 10 points, name this organ beneath the liver that stores bile.

tossups.p: This organ is divided into a rounded fundus, a body, and a narrow neck, which leads into the cystic duct. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct from the liver to form the common bile duct.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small organ that stores and concentrates bile, where gallstones can form.

tossups.p: Doctors check for Murphy’s sign, named for the surgeon John B. Murphy, by pressing below the right ribs as a patient breathes in, to see whether this organ is inflamed. Inflammation of this organ, often caused by a stone blocking its duct, is called cholecystitis [“koh-luh-sis-TY-tis”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pear-shaped organ, which can be removed if gallstones form in it.

tossups.p: Ultrasound scans are usually the first test doctors use to look for stones in this organ, which show up as bright spots that cast dark “shadows” on the screen. Those stones can form when bile holds more cholesterol than it can dissolve.
tossups.r: Removing this organ is one of the most common surgeries. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile, where gallstones form.

tossups.p: This organ releases a fluid whose salts emulsify fats, breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets that the enzyme lipase can digest more easily. That fluid, which this organ stores but does not make, contains no digestive enzymes of its own.
tossups.r: The liver makes that fluid. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile until a fatty meal arrives.

tossups.p: A stone that slips out of this organ and blocks the common bile duct can cause jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes from a buildup of bilirubin [“bil-ih-ROO-bin”]. This organ sits in the upper right part of the abdomen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this small, pear-shaped organ that stores bile from the liver.

tossups.p: Starting in the late 1980s, surgeons began removing this organ through a few tiny cuts, using a camera on a thin tube, in a “laparoscopic” [“lap-uh-roh-SKOP-ik”] operation that soon became the usual method. The medical name for that operation is cholecystectomy [“koh-luh-sis-TEK-tuh-mee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and can be removed if stones form in it.

tossups.p: The greenish-yellow color of the fluid stored in this organ comes from pigments such as bilirubin, which forms when old red blood cells are broken down. That fluid is made by the liver and reaches this organ through the cystic duct.
tossups.r: Hardened lumps called gallstones can form inside it. For 10 points, name this pouch under the liver that stores and concentrates bile.

tossups.p: Most stones in this organ never cause symptoms, but a stone that blocks its outlet can cause a sudden pain under the right ribs, called biliary colic, often after a fatty meal.
tossups.r: Those stones are called gallstones. For 10 points, name this organ that stores bile and squeezes it into the small intestine.

tossups.p: Fluid from this organ and juice from the pancreas enter the duodenum together through an opening called the ampulla of Vater [“FAH-ter”]. A stone from this organ that gets stuck there can inflame the pancreas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ, which stores bile between meals and sits under the liver.

tossups.p: Between meals, this organ makes the fluid it stores several times stronger by pulling water out of it, so it needs to hold only a few tablespoons. A fatty meal makes this organ’s muscular walls squeeze.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organ that receives bile from the liver through the cystic duct.

A stone blocking the common bile duct can cause jaundice, a yellowing from a buildup of bilirubin
Inflammation of it, often from a stone blocking its duct, is called cholecystitis
Usually removed through a few tiny cuts in a laparoscopic operation called a cholecystectomy
Ultrasound is the usual first test for its stones, which show up as bright spots that cast shadows

The name cholecystokinin means “bile sac mover”
When it contracts, the sphincter of Oddi relaxes to let bile flow into the duodenum

King Goujian of Yue is said to have tasted gall every day to remember a defeat, the story behind a Chinese saying

Divided into a rounded fundus, a body, and a narrow neck
Murphy’s sign, named for surgeon John B. Murphy, is a test for an inflamed one
A stone blocking its outlet can cause biliary colic, a sudden pain that often comes after fatty meals

trap.title: Liver or gallbladder?
trap.body: The liver makes bile, but the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it, so a clue like “produces bile” wants the liver. The pancreas is a third neighbor whose duct meets the bile duct, and all three send juices into the duodenum. Gallstones themselves, or the bile duct a stone can block, are separate answers too.
trap.fix: “Makes” or “produces” bile means the liver. “Stores,” “concentrates,” or “squeezes out” bile, CCK making it contract, gallstones forming inside it, or a cholecystectomy means the gallbladder. Insulin or digestive enzymes mean the pancreas.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gallbladder (accept gall bladder; do not accept “liver” or “bile duct”)
